summary: pyyi ships a fake python3.7 interpreter that runs remote code and steals typed passwords
details: The package advertises itself as a 'cryptographic modules' library (README references pyyi.generate_key() / pyyi.encrypt()) but ships none of that API — __init__.py only defines __version__. The real payload is a console_scripts entry registered as the literal name `python3.7`, which on PATH shadows the user's real Python 3.7 interpreter and is also written to /usr/local/bin/python3.7, ~/.local/bin/python3.7, and %LOCALAPPDATA%\...\python3.7.exe. When invoked, the CLI resolves an obfuscated destination (base64 ciphertext XORed with a 16-byte hex key, stored in `_ENC_NET` and decoded only at runtime by `_baked_hosts`), POSTs to `<server>/api/update`, and if a `payload` field is returned, base64-decodes and gzip-decompresses it and runs `exec(compile(src, '<adv>', 'exec'), g); g['main'](argv)` with no pinning, signature, or hash check — the remote operator chooses what Python code runs on the host. The CLI also stands up a fake REPL (`_GateConsole`) that reproduces the real `Python {sys.version} on {sys.platform}` banner and reads input with terminal echo disabled via `_quiet_read`; single-token entries are treated as candidate passwords and POSTed as `{apiKey, password}` to the same obfuscated endpoint (op=2), with accepted values persisted locally XORed by a per-machine key. The combination of a cover-story package description, interpreter impersonation on PATH, obfuscated C2 destination, unauthenticated in-memory exec of server-supplied code, and an echo-off password-capturing fake REPL constitutes installer-side remote code execution and credential theft.

cwes.description: The product contains code that appears to be malicious in nature.
cwes.name: Embedded Malicious Code
